# Positioning and Growth Plan — Siddharth

Written from verified research. Where the evidence failed review, I say so rather than filling the gap with confidence. Two things you must resolve before you touch anything: **what "Pramaan" actually is**, and **what your appointment letter says your designation is, character for character**. Both are flagged in place below.

---

## 1. The one decision that matters

**Pick backend. Fuse AI into it as a modifier, not as a second identity. Demote Data Analyst to the indexed layer only. Drop FDE from current-cycle targeting entirely.**

One primary role noun. Everywhere a human reads you sequentially — headline, About opener, resume summary, DM — it says backend engineer and nothing else.

Why this and not the four-way split you asked for:

**Backend is the only one of the four with full-time production evidence.** Onextel, Jul–Dec 2025: Java/Spring Boot, 30+ REST endpoints, PostgreSQL tuning, Redis, Docker, on a system moving 10M+ messages a month. That is a real, checkable, defensible body of work. Everything else you want to claim rests on either an internship or on nothing.

**AI is not a second domain — it is downstream of the first.** swyx's founding definition of the AI Engineer role rests on the observation that there are roughly 5,000 LLM researchers and roughly 50 million software engineers, and that shipping AI products wants engineers rather than researchers. AI engineering is reachable *through* backend, not instead of it. And the demand signal is real: LinkedIn's own Economic Graph reported AI talent hiring in India up 59.5% year over year in its 2026 AI Labor Market Report, with the direction corroborated by Naukri's monthly index (magnitude soft — one reviewer flagged the JobSpeak sourcing, since the primary blog blocked fetching). So the AI claim goes in as a verb attached to backend work: *building and evaluating LLM features behind production APIs*. Not as a noun in the role slot.

**Data Analyst has to be demoted, and this is the part you will resist.** Your only evidence is an internship — Power BI, dashboards, EDA, KNN — competing against people who hold the title full-time. The overlap between your backend stack and a typical analyst stack is Python and SQL and nothing else; Spring Boot, Postgres tuning, Redis and Docker buy you nothing in that market. Demoting it costs you almost nothing, because LinkedIn's Keywords filter pulls from the whole profile page and its Skills filter matches *implicit* skills extracted from text in any section — summary, position descriptions, title, headline. So the internship entry plus Power BI / SQL / Exploratory Data Analysis as Skills keeps your analyst retrieval intact while your visible layer stays single-purpose. Note honestly: I do **not** have market-size data to justify the demotion — the posting datasets on analyst demand did not survive review. The argument is entirely about your evidence being thin there, not about the market being small. If Data Analyst is actually your preferred destination, that is a different plan — a substitution for backend, not an addition to it. Decide that now, not in month four.

**FDE has to go, and the reason is not you.** Palantir's own live FDSE job description asks for "1+ years of relevant, post-college work experience" — you are not out of band on paper. The problem is req supply: Palantir has no India engineering presence, Anthropic's FDE posting asks for 4+ years in a technical customer-facing role, and the India-based FDE-titled reqs that are abundant are Palantir Foundry implementation roles at services firms. The count of India FDE reqs you could plausibly hold is on the order of one to a few, against a backend/AI market measured in thousands. Section 5 handles what to do about it.

**The forcing constraint underneath all of this: 3 hours a week is a distribution budget, not a transformation budget.** The closest fully-documented peer transition I have — Sadanand Pai, ~6 years in QA at Infosys into a dev role in about five months — ran at 3 hours per weekday plus 12–16 hours per weekend. You cannot run four content lanes, four application streams and four skill-building tracks inside 180 minutes. One lane, compounding, is the only allocation that produces anything.

## 2. Your profile, rewritten

### Do these two things first (12 minutes, and they gate everything else)

1. **Fix the name.** LinkedIn says "Siddharth Kumar", your resume says "Siddharth Sharma". Nothing in LinkedIn Recruiter reconciles a name mismatch, and the name is the key a recruiter uses to move from a received resume to your profile. Pick the one on your government ID and use it on LinkedIn, resume, Naukri and GitHub. If both are legitimate, put the other in LinkedIn's former-name field. Two minutes.
2. **Read your appointment letter and last payslip.** Note the official designation exactly. Indian enterprise letters often carry a band designation ("Software Engineer", "Engineer I", "Associate Software Engineer") that differs from the functional project role. If your letter says a generic engineer title, that is your Experience title and this whole problem shrinks. If it genuinely says Automation Test Engineer, use the dual-title format below. Ten minutes, and it is the highest-value ten minutes in this document.

### Headline

Limit is 220 characters. Truncation in search results, connection requests and comment threads happens somewhere around the first 60–70 characters — that number is a consistent third-party measurement, not documented by LinkedIn, so treat the front of the string as the only reliably visible part rather than trusting an exact cutoff.

**Primary (149 characters) — use today:**

```
Backend Engineer — Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker | 30+ production REST endpoints on a platform doing 10M+ messages/month | Python, SQL
```

**Alternative (134 characters) — switch to this the day your eval repo is public and linked in Featured:**

```
Backend Engineer — Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL | Building and evaluating LLM features behind production APIs | Python, Redis, Docker
```

Do not ship the alternative before the artifact exists. "Building and evaluating LLM features" without a clickable repo behind it fails the defend-it test on the first screening call.

Deleted from your current headline and why: **SDET** (it sits at characters 11–14, inside every truncated view that exists, and removing it is not concealment — the Experience section one scroll down still shows the role); **"ML & Data Science Learner"** (ranks for nothing a recruiter types, and "Learner" is an explicit non-hirability signal); **"| Python developer |"** and the orphan pipe; **"Pramaan"** from position one until you tell me what it is.

**On Pramaan — open question, do not let this sit.** It currently occupies characters 1–7, the highest-value real estate on your profile, and nobody in this research could establish what it is. Three cases: (a) a real venture where you have shipped something to real users — then it belongs in Experience as its own entry with a title that is literally true, and it is arguably the most hireable item you own; (b) a real ongoing side build with no users yet — Projects entry, linked in Featured; (c) aspirational branding — delete it. Do not resolve this by guessing.

### About section

Positioning claim in the first ~200 characters, above the "see more" fold. Prose paragraphs, not a keyword dump. Roughly 1,900 characters, inside the 2,600 limit. Fill the two bracketed slots yourself.

```
Backend engineer, about a year in. I write Java and Spring Boot services: 30+ REST endpoints
shipped on a platform that handled 10M+ messages a month, PostgreSQL query and index tuning,
Redis caching, Docker.

That was at Onextel, July to December 2025. It is the work I am strongest at and the work I
want to keep doing.

Right now I am in a test-automation seat, building automation frameworks and CI tooling in
Java and Python, and I ran an evaluation of MCP-based agent tooling. It is engineering work
and it taught me things about how services fail that I would not have learned shipping
features. It is not where I am aiming.

On my own time I am building [ARTIFACT NAME] — an evaluation harness for LLM output. About 50
hand-labelled examples on one narrow task, deterministic checks plus an LLM-as-judge grader,
run across two models, with the rubric and the failure taxonomy written down in the README.
The repo is in Featured. If you want to know whether I actually understand something, open
that.

Earlier: a data-analyst internship — Power BI dashboards, exploratory analysis over SQL
datasets, a KNN model — and an IEEE-published paper on IoT and blockchain. B.E. Electronics,
MIT-WPU Pune, 2025. [PRAMAAN LINE, ONLY IF REAL.]

What I am looking for: backend engineering, or backend with AI work attached — Java/Spring
Boot or Python, services with real traffic, somewhere I can own an endpoint end to end. Pune,
Bengaluru, Hyderabad or remote.

Straight about where I am: one year of professional experience, six months of it writing
production backend code. I would rather be judged on the endpoints, the query plans and the
eval repo than on my current job title.
```

Note what this does structurally. The canonical strings a recruiter types — Java, Spring Boot, REST, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker, Python, SQL, Power BI — appear literally, in prose, attached to something you actually did. That matters because the Skills filter matches implicit skills extracted from text anywhere on the profile, not only from the Skills section.

If you want the customer-facing signal for later, the place for it is here in prose — "worked directly with the people using the service" if that is true — using the established vocabulary (Solutions Engineer, customer-facing engineer). Never "FDE" and never in a structural field.

### Experience entries

**Current role.** Title = your official designation from the appointment letter. If that letter says Automation Test Engineer, use one of these and nothing else:

- `Automation Test Engineer (Backend / Platform Engineering)`
- `Automation Test Engineer — Java, Spring Boot, CI/CD Platform`

Use the identical string on LinkedIn, resume and Naukri so all three match each other and match your payslip.

**Never write "Backend Engineer" or "Software Engineer" alone in this field.** The rule is clarification is allowed, promotion is not, and omitting the official title is itself the violation. The downside is asymmetric: designation-only mismatches usually survive Indian background verification, but "usually survives" is a terrible risk profile for something that detonates after you have already resigned. The parenthetical gets most of the benefit with none of the exposure. On application forms that ask for your title at your current employer, always enter the official designation.

Description: 2–3 bullets, and every bullet's object is a *system*, not a test artifact. Keep: frameworks you built, CI pipelines, containers, internal tooling with real users, the MCP evaluation. Delete: suite counts, coverage percentages, defects found, regression cycles, and Selenium/TestNG/Cypress as headline skills. Start each with Built / Designed / Instrumented. Write "built a Java-based automation framework and CI pipeline", not "performed testing".

Also run a literal find-and-remove pass across the whole profile for: `QA`, `Quality Assurance`, `Manual Testing`, `Test Cases`, `Defect`, `Bug Report`, `Regression Suite`. Keep `SDET` and `Test Automation` — both are engineering-register and both are defensible. **Flag this one honestly: the reason is that some published backend sourcing strings carry `NOT ("QA" OR ...)` clauses, and I could not confirm how common that actually is.** The mechanism is certain (Keywords pulls from the whole profile page, NOT is supported, so a NOT term anywhere removes you from that result set entirely); the prevalence is unknown. It is a 20-minute experiment, not a certainty. Do not contort the profile further on the strength of it.

**Onextel (Jul–Dec 2025).** Exact title as it was — Junior Software Engineer. Exact dates. This entry carries your resume, so it gets **5–6 bullets against the current role's 2–3**. Bullet volume is the one ordering signal you control without touching chronology, which you cannot break.

Shape every bullet as *built \<artifact\> using \<named stack\> handling \<number\>*, and use a number you can defend under questioning:

> 30+ production REST endpoints in ~6 months on a platform handling 10M+ messages/month; cut p95 latency through PostgreSQL index and query tuning plus Redis caching.

**The scale figure is the one place you can quietly destroy yourself.** State 10M+ messages/month as *the environment*, never as *your authorship*. Pre-commit to one sentence and never contradict it in writing: "The system handled 10M+ messages a month; I built and shipped 30+ REST endpoints in it." You did not design for that scale and must never imply you did.

Also write and rehearse a 25-second answer to "why did Onextel end after six months" — one sentence of factual reason, one sentence of what you wanted next, stop. Put it in your interview-intel file.

**Data Analyst internship.** Its own entry, the word `Intern` in the title, accurate start and end dates. Recruiter's Years-of-Experience filter counts total years across the whole profile, so completeness is worth something and date padding is checkable against the same records a verifier uses. Description carries the real tooling: Power BI, exploratory analysis, SQL, KNN.

**Pramaan / the side product.** Only if it is real and ongoing. Its own current Experience entry (or a Projects entry if there is no venture), title literally true of what you do, dated from when you actually started, description naming the real stack and one shipped thing. LinkedIn does let you reorder concurrent current positions — but the claim that this changes the "current title" a recruiter preview shows did not survive review, so do it because the entry is true and useful, not as a ranking trick. **Never invent a second concurrent position at your employer.** It overstates, colleagues can see it, and it touches employer detail you must not publish.

### Skills section, in order

Pin as your top skills, in this order, as many slots as your account offers:

```
1. Java
2. Spring Boot
3. REST APIs
4. PostgreSQL
5. Python
```

Then, in order:

```
SQL · Redis · Docker · Microservices · Query Optimization · Distributed Systems ·
Git · Linux · CI/CD · Power BI · Exploratory Data Analysis · pandas · Data Analysis ·
Test Automation · API Testing
```

Rules that matter more than the list:

- **Never pin a test or QA skill.** Keep them present — removing them would be dishonest and reads as an eight-month hole — but keep them at the bottom.
- **Associate each skill with the specific Experience or Project entry where you used it**, using the checkboxes LinkedIn offers. This is what LinkedIn itself now recommends in place of the retired Skill Assessments.
- **Do not add LLMOps, AutoML or Prompt Engineering.** They are in LinkedIn's own published India top-five rising skill stacks, which is exactly why every guru will tell you to add them, and you cannot survive fifteen minutes on any of the three. This is the single highest-risk unforced error available to you.
- **Add "Model Context Protocol (MCP)" only if** you can explain the protocol's transport, tool-schema shape and failure modes unprompted. Otherwise leave MCP in the Experience description as an activity you performed, not as a claimed skill.
- **Add "Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)" only after** the eval project is public.
- **The defend-it test, applied to every skill on the profile:** can you state one design decision you personally made with it and one thing that went wrong? If not, it comes off.

### Featured section

2–4 items, and every one must be a link a stranger can click and verify in thirty seconds:

1. The eval repo (once it exists) — README with the rubric, the failure taxonomy, and the command to reproduce.
2. Your strongest Java/Spring Boot repo with a real README.
3. The IEEE publication.
4. Pramaan / the side product, if it is shipped and reachable.

The stat everyone cites for the Featured section — "64% of 1,200 recruiters said it was a difference-maker, Resume Worded 2024" — does not exist. A targeted search for that survey returns nothing and the figure appears only on blogs selling resume tooling. Same for the "recommendations get 14x more views" cluster. Do the Featured section anyway, because it is thirty minutes and it is the only place above the fold where a verifiable link can live. Do not do it because of a number.

**Recommendations:** two is enough, from named Onextel colleagues who can speak to backend delivery. Two specific ones beat six vague ones. Do not chase volume, and do not script their wording.

### Open to Work

Set it to **"Recruiters only"**, never "All LinkedIn members". This puts you in the Recruiter Open-to-Work Spotlight without the public green frame — LinkedIn states plainly that a candidate sharing with recruiters only "will still appear in an Open to work spotlight search; however, the #OPENTOWORK photo frame won't display."

In the preference fields list, in order: **Backend Engineer, Software Engineer, AI Engineer, Data Analyst, Forward Deployed Engineer.** This is the only place FDE and Data Analyst appear as role nouns anywhere on your profile. Locations: Pune + Bengaluru + Hyderabad + remote. Fill the India-specific notice-period field.

**Delete any QA/SDET/test title from those preferences.** Those fields are what feed recruiter inbound, and leaving them in keeps the wrong inbound coming.

**The honest caveat, which is yours to decide:** LinkedIn says it "takes steps to prevent LinkedIn Recruiter users who work at your current company from seeing your shared career interests" but that it "cannot guarantee complete privacy." That disclaimer appears twice on their own help page. This is the only recommendation in this section with a real downside. If any employer-visibility risk is unacceptable to you, skip it — do not let me tell you it is safe.

### The cheap, uncontroversial rest

One clear, well-lit, front-facing photo, plain background, face filling most of the frame — then stop. Trait judgments from faces form in about 100ms and do not meaningfully change with more looking (Willis & Todorov, *Psychological Science* 2006). Every specific prescription about smiling, squinting or jacket colour traces to a company selling photo scoring. Banner at 1584x396 with content kept inside a centred safe area, carrying one plain line of proof. Custom URL set once and never changed. Complete LinkedIn's workplace and government-ID verification (verification does not publish an employer-directory title that could contradict your Experience field).

## 3. What to post

### The tension, stated honestly

You asked for honesty here, so: **the claim that technical depth costs reach did not survive review.** It rested on three observed posts, which is an anecdote, not a measurement. I am not going to tell you deep content underperforms.

What did survive is worse for the "grow an audience" objective:

- **There is no evidence, in any form, that LinkedIn content affects hiring outcomes for 1–2 YOE engineers in India.** The research looked specifically for it and found nothing — not a study, not a dataset, not a recruiter survey.
- **No verified case exists of a 1–4 YOE Indian engineer hired into backend/AI because of a following.** Every large India-market technical audience traced back to someone who already held the credential: six years of ML and three patents, a Senior PM role at Google Cloud, IIT-BHU, three years at Deloitte, or a course business. That is absence of evidence, not proof of absence — but it is what there is.
- **Nothing in LinkedIn's documented Recruiter filter set searches personal follower count, creator status, post content or a Top Voice badge.** The filters are titles, keywords over profile text, skills, companies, schools, locations, seniority, years, spotlights. (LinkedIn refuses to document its ranking function, so I cannot tell you nothing content-shaped enters ranking — only that nothing content-shaped enters the documented retrieval.)
- Meanwhile the genres that reliably grow a LinkedIn audience — milestone, gratitude, journey, career-advice — are the genres with zero evidence of hiring value and some evidence of harm. The cleanest available experiment (Frontiers in Psychology 2025, n=480 managers and HR specialists, randomised) found that for a *highly qualified* candidate, unprofessional social content dropped hiring intention from 4.48 to 3.60 (F = 92.28, p < 0.001) while professional content lifted it only to 4.69. Caveat it properly: that sample was Turkish hospitality HR, so transfer to Indian tech hiring is my assumption, not the study's finding.

**So the resolution is: content is capped, not central. 45 minutes a week, one post, and it is the first thing cut in a compressed week — applications are the last.** It feels like the opposite, because a post feels like progress and an application feels like a lottery ticket. It is the opposite.

### The three pillars

**Pillar 1 — "I measured this myself" (majority of posts).** A benchmark you ran on your own machine, with the repo, the command line, the versions and the hardware, so a skeptic can reproduce it. Example shape: *"I wanted to see whether Redis pipelining mattered at small batch sizes, so I measured it: 1,000 individual GETs took 380ms, pipelined took 12ms. I expected the crossover below 5 keys. It wasn't."*

**Pillar 2 — postmortem of your own side project (once a month).** Fixed five lines: what you built and what broke, with the symptom as a number; what you thought the cause was; what it actually was; why your design made that failure possible; what you still do not understand. End on the unknown. Do not use the word "journey" and do not thank anyone.

**Pillar 3 — "I read the primary source" (occasional).** Reproduce one specific number from a paper or an official benchmark and report whether you got it. This is the single move from your sister's playbook that transfers completely to 1 YOE, because it claims no seniority at all.

### What of Hritika's register you can honestly borrow

**Transfers:** the numbered specific opening claim; one short sentence per line with nothing over about twelve words; a memorable closing line instead of a summary; and above all her research discipline of reading the primary benchmark paper before writing.

**Does not transfer:** the implied first-person production authority of "here is what broke in production" on Flink or WASM internals. She is a Data Architect writing to an audience built over years. A 1-YOE engineer in that register is not merely unconvincing, it is checkable, and it will be checked.

**Also does not transfer: the seven hashtags.** Cut to 0–3, and only genuinely specific ones (#PostgreSQL, #SpringBoot) — never #Tech, #Coding, #Engineering. LinkedIn's product chief said in July 2025 that hashtags are not essential because the feed models now read post text directly. The specific "no hashtags outperform by 5–10%" figures come from a consultant who sells LinkedIn training and publishes no raw data, so ignore the magnitude and just stop spending lines on them.

**What substitutes for production war stories you do not have**, ranked by credibility per hour:

1. Benchmarks you ran yourself, published with the repo and the command line — highest, because falsifiable and claiming no seniority.
2. Reproducing one number from a primary source and reporting whether you got it.
3. A bug you personally found and root-caused in your own code, written as a postmortem naming the wrong assumption.
4. Numbers you are quoting *with attribution* from a named primary source — never an unattributed "systems like this typically".

**Two hard register rules.** Every number in a post is either one you personally produced or one you attribute. Every opening line states what you *did* or *read*, not what you *know*. "Here's what breaks when you scale Postgres" becomes "I ran pgbench against my own box with and without a connection pooler. Here are the p95 numbers." Same structure, defensible claim.

**Keep a numbers file.** Every time you measure anything — a latency, a query plan, a benchmark, a bug's blast radius — it goes in with the date and the method. Posts are drafted *from that file only*, never from scratch. Five minutes per entry, and it removes the hard part of drafting.

### Mechanics that are actually documented

- **Line one carries the payload.** LinkedIn's production ranker predicts long dwell as a first-class objective and discounts posts by predicted skip probability. And Dan Roth stated in Feb 2024 that LinkedIn *stopped* using "read more" clicks as a value signal: they had "incorrectly attributed the 'read more' button as a signal that people were getting some value." Curiosity-gap hooks now farm a click that has been removed from the ranker, and cost credibility with engineers on top.
- **Never let an LLM write the post.** A large-sample study (Pangram Labs, ~1M posts, July 2026) classified over 40% of LinkedIn long-form posts as fully AI-generated — single study, unaudited by me. The load-bearing part is LinkedIn's response, which is separately reported: on 30 July 2026 they shipped a "Seems like AI slop" report button that reduces out-of-network visibility and privately notifies the poster, and they removed their own "enhance your post" tool. Engineers are the audience most likely to press that button. Using AI to fact-check or critique your own draft is fine; generating the prose is not.
- **Four humanness markers per post:** one ugly non-round number you measured (41ms, 2.7s, 1,743 rows — never "about 40% faster"); named tool versions and hardware; one first-person specific only you could write; one honest open question at the end.
- **Put the link in the post body, not the first comment.** The sources conflict here — a LinkedIn product director says there is no intentional penalty for external links, a consultant selling LinkedIn training says a body link cuts median reach 18.8%. Neither is strong. I am picking body because verification is the entire mechanism by which your content converts, and hiding the link adds friction to exactly that step. Treat it as unresolved and low-stakes.

### Cadence

**One post a week. Two maximum. Never daily.** 45 minutes, drafted from the numbers file. That is the whole content allocation.

### Pre-publish checklist, three questions, every time

1. Could any sentence here be traced to a specific internal system, incident, tool, team size, client or industry at my employer? If yes, **cut it — not soften it, cut it.**
2. Is every number here from a repo, dataset or benchmark I can hand a stranger?
3. Would I defend every claim here in a 45-minute interview with a staff engineer? Anything failing this gets rewritten as an observation, not a claim.

Screeners explicitly hunt for sharing of confidential information as a red flag. This checklist also means all your content must come from side projects and public data — which is a constraint that happens to point at exactly the right content anyway.

### What to track instead of followers

Three numbers, weekly, five minutes:
1. Profile views (LinkedIn shows this).
2. Inbound DMs from engineers or hiring managers that reference a specific post or repo.
3. Comments from people whose own headline says Backend / Platform / SRE / ML / Data.

And one number that matters more than all three: **non-QA recruiter conversations started.** If that is still zero after four weeks of a fixed profile, the profile is the bottleneck, not your coding and not your posting.

## 4. Top Voice: the honest answer

**No. Retire it as a goal today, and do not put it in the 24-week plan as a milestone or a KPI.**

The facts, all from LinkedIn's own pages or a dated dataset:

- **The route most people mean is closed.** LinkedIn retired the gold Community Top Voice badge and discontinued earning it through collaborative articles starting 8 October 2024; existing badges expired within 60 days and all were gone by 7 December 2024. Collaborative articles are still live in 2026 and still solicit contributions — they now award nothing. Their stated reason included that contributions had become generic or AI-generated.
- **The surviving blue badge has no executable criteria.** It is invite-only for "experts, leaders, changemakers, public figures, and innovators", assessed twice a year by LinkedIn's team, held for a minimum of six months with renewal conditional. No threshold, no score, no follower minimum, no application produces it.
- **The cohort is executives, not creators.** Across all 368 new Top Voices in 31 countries in May 2026: 58% hold executive positions, including 121 CEOs, 62 founders, 25 presidents or chairs. Exactly **two** people list "Content Creator" as their title. India received 20 of the 368 slots. None of the editors' picks featured for the January 2026 class was a technical individual contributor. (Source caveat: this is a vendor's dataset published without raw data. I weight it up because it is specific, dated, falsifiable, and argues *against* the vendor's own commercial interest.)
- **Not one measured or credible source connects the badge to a hiring outcome.** No study, no dataset, no recruiter survey, no A/B evidence. The claims that exist — badge holders appear more in searches, posting 3+ times a week gets 2–3x more recruiter outreach, polls increase visibility 40% among recruiters — appear only on blogs of companies selling LinkedIn tools or coaching, with no sample, method or date.
- **The one lever that would move you toward eligibility is founder framing** — and it directly undermines being hired as a 1-YOE backend engineer. Your headline already leads with a venture. Keep it engineering-first.

You are not a long-shot candidate for this. You are outside the population being assessed.

### What to pursue instead

Replace it with falsifiable goals you control:

- **By month 6: three named backend/AI hiring managers or senior engineers in Pune or Bengaluru know your name well enough to reply to a DM.**
- **By month 6: at least five comments on your posts from people whose headline contains Backend / Platform / SRE / ML / Data, and at least two inbound conversations referencing a specific post or repo.**
- Authority credentials that survive scrutiny because they are tied to artifacts: a merged PR in a library you actually use, an accepted meetup or lightning talk in Pune, a benchmark someone else cites.
- **Connections, not followers.** A connection automatically becomes a follower in both directions, so this is a fully controllable lever: 20 minutes a week sending 10–15 personalised connection requests to backend/AI engineers and engineering managers at target companies, each with a one-line note referencing something specific they built or posted. That is roughly 500–700 relevant new first-degree connections a year — people who both see your feed and could refer you. Never automate this and never buy it.

And never put "content creator", "thought leader", "top voice" or a follower count anywhere on your profile. The achievement is allowed to be visible; the identity is not.

## 5. FDE: the honest answer

**Not reachable now, and the constraint is req supply, not your profile.** That distinction matters, because otherwise you will read the silence as a profile problem and keep rewriting a profile that is fine.

Palantir's own live FDSE description asks for "1+ years of relevant, post-college work experience", names no customer-facing requirement, and lists as its only hard technical bar "Strong coder with shown proficiency in programming languages such as Python, Java, C++, TypeScript/JavaScript, or similar." On paper you are not out of band. But Palantir has no India engineering presence, Anthropic's FDE posting requires 4+ years in a technical customer-facing role, OpenAI's India deployment roles gate well above your level, and the India FDE-titled reqs that *are* abundant are Palantir Foundry implementation roles at services firms. The count of India-based FDE reqs you could plausibly hold is on the order of one to a few, against thousands of backend/AI reqs.

Your existing work is also more FDE-shaped than you are presenting it. Palantir's FDSE responsibilities are literally wrangling large-scale data, developing custom applications tailored to customer needs, and driving projects from ideation to deployment. First Round Review's piece on hiring FDEs — built on interviews with an ex-Palantir hiring lead and Ironclad's — names "compulsive builders" (people who are prolific: built a tool, released an app, contributed to open source) and "outcome-oriented, independent thinkers" not doing a lot of pattern matching, and notes that candidates with 10+ years at FAANG were treated as a red flag. Which means the FDE gate you should be building is the same one that makes you a better backend hire.

### What to do about it

1. **Zero FDE language in the headline, the About opening, or any Experience title.** "Forward deployed" appears in essentially no India backend or AI JD. Every character spent on it is a character not matching a query that would surface you, and the headline is a single shared resource across all searches. The words go in the Open-to-Work preference list and nowhere else.
2. **Keep it as a 15-minute-a-month apply-only channel.** A saved LinkedIn search for "forward deployed", plus a monthly check of `jobs.lever.co/palantir` and `sarvam.ai/careers`. Fire off the international Palantir reqs if you want a lottery ticket; budget nothing beyond that.
3. **Verify Sarvam yourself.** They are the one India-headquartered company that surfaced with FDE-titled engineering roles at a band you could stretch to, but their careers page would not render its JD text for me on two attempts, so **I have no verified posting text and you should not plan around the band I could not read.** Open it in a browser this week. While you are there, follow three to five Sarvam engineers — reading what they say about deployments is free intelligence and costs nothing from your budget.
4. **Ship the side product publicly, even minimally.** Under First Round's own rubric, "released an app" is a named screening criterion, and an unshipped project scores zero on it. This is the highest-leverage FDE action available to you and it is also the highest-leverage backend action, which is why it is the one build in this plan.
5. **Do one 90-minute exercise that pays into three targets at once.** Take the Onextel messaging platform and write a one-page graceful-degradation plan for 10x load: which endpoints you shed, what you serve stale from Redis, what you queue, how the client learns capability is reduced. That single page is FDE scenario prep, backend system-design prep, and post material. (The published details of Palantir's interview loop did not survive verification, so treat the exercise as a good use of ninety minutes rather than as targeted prep for a known format. And do not buy any FDE course, certification or interview guide — every India FDE salary band in circulation traces to sites selling FDE career guides, and one widely-quoted growth figure surfaces in a press release launching a paid FDE credential.)
6. **Know what the abundant India "FDE" reqs are before you apply.** The thirty-second tell: if the required-skills list names a vendor platform (Foundry, AIP) rather than a language or a problem, it is implementation work. That is a judgment call with a real cost — it adds a vendor-platform specialisation to a history you are already trying to un-label — not an automatic no. And if an FDE offer ever does materialise, screen it on one question: does this team own product surface that ships to many customers, or does it configure a platform for one?

Realistic timeline: FDE is a 3-year destination reached *through* backend or AI engineering. Revisit at 3–4 YOE with real production LLM deployment work behind you. The requirement lists at Anthropic and OpenAI double as a build list you can start on today with nobody's permission: advanced prompt engineering, agent development, evaluation frameworks.

---

## 6. 90 days

Two separate budgets. Do not let them blur.

**Budget A — 3 hours/week (the stated ceiling).** Profile, applications, referrals, one post.
**Budget B — a named weekend block, 3–5 hours/week for about six weeks.** The eval artifact. This does **not** fit inside Budget A and I am not going to pretend it does. If Budget B does not exist, cut the post to zero and keep applications — a smaller account pointing at a real artifact beats a larger one pointing at nothing, and applications beat both.

**Standing weekly shape from week 4 onward (180 min):** 60 min applications · 20 min referral asks · 15 min Naukri touch + tracker · 45 min one post · 40 min buffer that interview prep consumes once interviews are live.

| Week | Budget A (3h) | Budget B (weekend) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Name field + custom URL (10m). Read appointment letter, note exact designation (10m). Resolve Pramaan (10m). New headline + Experience titles + dates (40m). Open to Work, recruiters-only, target titles (15m). First 8 applications (75m). | Scope the eval project: pick one narrow task, decide the two models. |
| 2 | Rewrite About in full (60m). Onextel description, 5–6 bullets with defensible numbers (45m). Current-role description, 2–3 system bullets (30m). 8 applications (45m). | Hand-label the first ~25 examples. |
| 3 | Skills section + associate each skill with its entry (40m). Featured with what exists today (20m). QA-term find-and-remove pass (20m). Photo/banner if needed (20m). 10 applications (60m). Open the numbers file (5m). | Finish labelling to ~50. Write the rubric down. |
| 4 | Standing shape begins. 12 applications. 20 referral asks. Naukri. **First post** — the pgbench or Redis-pipelining shape, from the numbers file. | Deterministic checks working. |
| 5 | Standing shape. Rehearse the Onextel six-months answer and the 10M+ environment sentence (20m from buffer). | LLM-as-judge grader. |
| 6 | Standing shape. Ask two Onextel colleagues for recommendations (10m). | Run across both models; record the failure taxonomy. |
| 7 | Standing shape. Post #4. | README: rubric, taxonomy, reproduce command. **Publish.** |
| 8 | **Switch headline to the alternative.** Add the repo to Featured and to About. Add RAG to Skills. Post: the error-analysis post — what labelling 50 examples actually taught you. | Buffer / fix what the README exposed. |
| 9 | Standing shape. Post #6. Write the 10x degradation one-pager (90m, from buffer + post slot). | Small backend repo cleanup — README that a stranger can run. |
| 10 | Standing shape. First monthly postmortem of the eval project. Check the FDE saved search and Sarvam (15m). | Ship the side product publicly, even minimally. |
| 11 | Standing shape. Post #8. | Side product: one shipped thing, linkable. |
| 12 | Standing shape. Post #9. Review the application tracker: response rate, and non-QA recruiter conversations started. | Buffer. |
| 13 | **Decision week.** If non-QA conversations are still zero at ~110 applications: the resume or the targeting is broken, and volume will not fix it — take the resume to two working backend engineers for a line-by-line read. If interviews are live: everything except applications gets cut, buffer plus post slot go to interview prep and the degradation one-pager becomes your system-design story. | Whatever the interviews demand. |

**Application rules that make the 60 minutes work.** Turn the experience-level filter OFF and search by JD text instead — apply to anything written "1–3 years", "2–4 years" or "2+ years". Hard rule: **if the stack matches and the years do not, apply; if the years match and the stack does not, skip.** Locations Pune + Bengaluru + Hyderabad + remote, never Pune alone. Prioritise backend JDs that name testing, TDD/ATDD, CI/CD or code-quality ownership among the responsibilities — on those, your current role satisfies a stated requirement instead of contradicting the role, and one current-role bullet should name the automation work directly in the JD's own phrasing. Weight toward referral and direct-to-hiring-manager routes over Easy Apply, because the screen is where the title penalty fires. Twelve a week is a floor, not a ceiling, and do not cut it in response to a layoff headline.

**Referral asks.** One 20-minute batch a week, fired within about three days of a trigger (the req going live, the person posting that their team is hiring, the person changing jobs). Never a bare connection request — always a short note naming the specific req and your actual stack. Never to anyone at your current employer, and never name your employer in one. Expect very few replies and do not read the rate as a signal about your profile: **there is no evidence that the profile is the variable in cold referral response, and every cold-outreach number in circulation comes from B2B sales vendors measuring sales prospecting.**

**One thing that happens inside paid hours, not this budget.** Ask your lead to own bug fixes in the product code you already test — framed as improving your test design, which is true and easy to say yes to. Then ask for one small feature or service. Track landed non-test commits as a number. That number is what makes both an internal case and an external resume bullet, and it is the route that actually worked in nearly every first-hand account I have. Keep all of it out of every public channel.

**One deadline, written at the top of your career-prep file.** By a date you pick — I would use 31 March 2027 — you are either in a role whose official designation is not test-related, or you have six-plus months of shipped non-test engineering work inside your current seat that a manager will vouch for.

## 7. Do NOT do these

1. **Do not put "Backend Engineer" or "Software Engineer" alone in your current Experience title.** Clarification survives verification; inflation does not, and it detonates after you have resigned. The parenthetical dual-title gets most of the benefit with none of the exposure.
2. **Do not take a "Backend QA Engineer" or "Sr. QA Engineer — Backend Focus" role.** These are real, currently-posted title categories. They will feel like progress because they contain the word "backend", and they are the gravity well: a second test-titled role makes the "backend engineer temporarily in a test seat" story permanently unavailable.
3. **Do not try to erase testing entirely.** Your title is one click from every post. A profile that never mentions test work reads as an eight-month hole plus a contradiction — worse than a reframed truth. Reframe the system-building slice, delete the test-artifact metrics, keep the title visible and unemphasised.
4. **Do not add LLMOps, AutoML or Prompt Engineering to Skills.** They are literally in LinkedIn's India top-five rising stacks, which is why every guru will push them, and a punctured AI claim at a 2-YOE interview is unrecoverable.
5. **Do not put FDE anywhere structural** — not the headline, not the About opening, not a title. It matches no India backend JD and it spends a shared resource.
6. **Do not contribute to LinkedIn collaborative articles.** The badge they awarded was retired 8 Oct 2024 and gone from the app by 7 Dec 2024. The articles are still live and still soliciting. It is now unpaid, uncredited content production, and the in-product invitations plus stale guru guides both still point at it.
7. **Do not take LinkedIn Skill Assessments.** LinkedIn wound them down and deleted the badges from profiles. Any source still recommending them is unmaintained — use it as a credibility filter on that source.
8. **Do not chase follower count** as a proxy for either objective. The badge has decoupled from audience size, nothing in the documented Recruiter filter set searches personal followers, and a follower who is not a hiring manager, engineer or potential referrer is worth approximately nothing to you.
9. **Do not post daily,** and do not feel behind for posting once a week. The step from 1 to 2–4 posts a week is where any gain is; daily costs reach per post. Your 3-hour ceiling is close to the optimum here, not a handicap.
10. **Do not let an LLM write your posts,** and do not use curiosity-gap hooks, "👇", or broetry ladders. The click those hooks farm was removed from the ranker in Feb 2024, and the slop-report button exists since 30 July 2026.
11. **Do not post progress logs, explainers or listicles.** "Day 26 of my DSA journey", "Excited to share I completed X", "Here's how Kafka works", "5 things every backend dev must know". The first contains no falsifiable claim; the second and third assert authority you cannot defend at 1 YOE and the market is saturated with AI-generated versions. Reproduce and measure instead of explain.
12. **Do not post anything sourced from your current employer,** including anonymised or industry-level hints. Screeners hunt specifically for shared confidential information, and one bad signal can swamp demonstrated competence.
13. **Do not use engagement pods.** They produce exactly the generic comments the ranker discounts, plus the automated-comment behaviour LinkedIn is now blocking.
14. **Do not write "T-shaped", "generalist", "versatile", "multi-disciplinary", "thought leader", "content creator" or "Learner" anywhere.** No recruiter filters on any of them and they read as filler. If asked about breadth in an interview, the defensible line is causal, not shape-based: "backend is where I've shipped production code; the analytics and test-automation work is why I know what breaks downstream."
15. **Do not invent a second concurrent position at your employer** to exploit LinkedIn's current-position reordering. The mechanic is real; it is only clean when the added position is genuinely your own.
16. **Do not front-load LeetCode and system design.** Multiple first-hand accounts describe grinding for months before discovering the bottleneck was interview *acquisition*, not interview performance. When non-QA interviews are actually happening, it becomes the priority. Before then it is displacement.
17. **Do not buy** Naukri Premium on the strength of "paid profiles rank higher" (only sources are Naukri and its affiliates — get the free mechanics working for eight weeks and measure first), FDE courses or interview guides, photo-scoring tools, or any LinkedIn growth product.
18. **Do not filter job searches by experience level, and do not restrict to Pune.** Both hide the band that is actually your market.
19. **Discard on sight** any LinkedIn advice that mentions "Creator Mode" (retired March 2024), treats the gold/Community Top Voice badge as attainable, or quotes a follower threshold for the blue badge. It is a staleness test that costs seconds and saves hours.
20. **Do not treat any percentage figure for the "QA title penalty" as real.** No résumé-audit or callback study isolating a QA/test title in engineering hiring exists. Anyone quoting a number — especially anyone selling career coaching — is inventing it.

---

## 8. What is known vs what is a bet

### Known — primary, first-party, verifiable

- **Recruiter's Job titles filter is fed by titles in the Experience section, not the headline.** Keywords pulls from the whole profile page and supports Boolean. Job functions derive from job titles. Seniority derives from your position level at your current company. Years of experience is a whole-profile total, and there is no filter for years-in-a-specific-role. (LinkedIn Recruiter Help, read directly.)
- **The Skills filter matches implicit skills** — "extracted from text within any section of the member's profile, such as the summary, position description, title, and headline" — not only the Skills section.
- **Open to Work has a "Recruiters only" mode** that puts you in the Spotlight without the public frame, exposing structured desired-title fields plus India-specific notice-period and expected-salary fields. LinkedIn's own page states twice that it "cannot guarantee complete privacy."
- **Recruiters cannot re-sort search results.** Boolean is AND/OR/NOT/quotes/parentheses only; braces, brackets and wildcards are unsupported.
- **Skill Assessments were wound down and the badges deleted from profiles.** LinkedIn's replacement guidance is to tag skills to specific jobs, projects and credentials.
- **The collaborative-article Top Voice badge is gone** (discontinued 8 Oct 2024, all badges removed by 7 Dec 2024). The blue badge is invite-only with no published threshold and a six-month reviewable tenure.
- **Zero sources of any quality connect a Top Voice badge to a hiring outcome.**
- **LinkedIn stopped using "read more" clicks as a value signal** (Dan Roth, Feb 2024), and its production ranker predicts long dwell while discounting predicted skip.
- **LinkedIn shipped a "Seems like AI slop" report button on 30 July 2026** and removed its own "enhance your post" writing tool.
- **Palantir's FDSE JD asks 1+ years post-college**; Anthropic's FDE posting asks 4+ years in a technical customer-facing role. India-located FDE reqs at services firms ask for Palantir Foundry and AIP experience.
- **Naukri holds roughly 118 million resumes with ~25,000 new profiles and ~850,000 profile modifications a day** — the resume inventory Indian recruiters actually query.
- **LinkedIn's own India outputs:** AI talent hiring up 59.5% YoY (AI Labor Market Report 2026); the Skills on the Rise 2026 engineering top ten (Querying, Cybersecurity, Programming, LLMOps, Workflow Automation, Process Optimisation, Collaboration, Data Engineering, AutoML, API).
- **Trait judgments from a face form in about 100ms** and do not meaningfully change with longer looking (Willis & Todorov, *Psychological Science* 2006, peer-reviewed).
- **The Featured-section stat everyone cites is fabricated.** "64% of 1,200 recruiters, Resume Worded 2024" returns nothing on targeted search and appears only on blogs selling resume tools. Same for the "14x more profile views" recommendations cluster.

### Bets — judgment, thin evidence, or evidence that only came from people selling something

- **That the QA-title penalty is real and lands at resume screen.** Direction is supported by convergent first-hand accounts across roughly ten independent anonymous threads, which is worth something. But they are anonymous, US-centric, mostly 4–10 YOE, from a forum whose culture actively bashes QA — and **no measured callback or audit study isolating a QA title in engineering hiring exists.** Direction: I would act on it. Magnitude: unknown, and unknowable from what is published.
- **That `NOT ("QA" OR "tester")` clauses are common in real backend sourcing strings.** Low confidence — the one page fetched verbatim showed only `NOT "Frontend"`. The mechanism is certain, the prevalence is not.
- **That LinkedIn content helps you get hired at all.** No evidence in any form for 1–2 YOE engineers in India, and no verified case of a 1–4 YOE Indian engineer hired because of a following. This is the single largest gap in the whole research, and it is why content is capped at 45 minutes and cut first.
- **That the dual-title format survives Indian background verification.** The BGV material is Glassdoor/Fishbowl/Grapevine forum chatter, not policy documents. Verify against your own appointment letter and relieving-letter language, not against my sourcing.
- **Everything about how LinkedIn weights profile fields.** LinkedIn documents nothing. Every confident claim you will read ("the headline is indexed at 5x", "recent titles weigh far more") comes from LinkedIn-optimisation newsletters and recruiting-SaaS content marketing. Also: the LinkedIn title-standardisation taxonomy claim did not survive review as a current, load-bearing mechanic, so do not build anything on "what standardized title SDET maps to."
- **Headline and About truncation thresholds (~60–70 chars, ~200–300 chars).** Consistent across many independent third-party measurements, documented by LinkedIn nowhere, device- and locale-dependent, and liable to change silently.
- **That a second concurrent current position changes what recruiters see.** The reorder mechanic is documented and real; the claim that it changes the "current title" in a recruiter preview was rejected in review. Add the entry because it is true and useful, not as a ranking play.
- **The weekly Naukri "freshness" touch.** The Resdex last-modified ordering mechanic traces to a 2016 page and an SEO blog. It costs two minutes a week, so do it — but do not believe the mechanism until you see the response rate move.
- **Referral share-of-hires numbers.** No India-specific measurement of what share of junior tech hires come from referrals exists. Every circulating figure ("40% of hires", "referrals are 7% of applicants") traces to US recruiting-software vendors recycling pre-2020 Jobvite data with no Indian sample. What *is* real and dated: Indian employers currently pay cash referral bonuses (Infosys announced ₹10,000–50,000 per successful referral in Sept 2025), which is why the ask works at all.
- **Cold-outreach response rates.** All of it from B2B sales-automation vendors measuring sales prospecting, not referral asks. The "InMail gets 18–25% replies" figure comes from agencies selling LinkedIn outreach.
- **The junior-rung ratio (5.9% entry-level vs 50.1% senior) and all Data-Analyst market-size numbers.** One dataset with disclosed methodology, and reviewers split on whether to accept it. The *shape* — a senior-heavy posting mix, Bengaluru several times Pune's volume — is probably right. The ratios are soft. The action (filter off, apply by JD text) is correct either way because it is free.
- **All algorithm-format numbers** (hashtag penalties, posting-cadence curves, the 18.8% link penalty). Largest sample in the niche, but published by a consultant selling LinkedIn training, unauditable, and reporting engagement rate rather than reach. Directional at best.
- **The Frontiers hiring-intention experiment.** Real, randomised, n=480 — but Turkish hospitality HR. Transfer to Indian tech hiring is my assumption.
- **The AI-slop prevalence figure (40%+ of long-form posts).** One study, unaudited by me. LinkedIn's product response is the part I would rely on.
- **The Top Voice cohort composition.** A vendor's dataset published without raw data. I weight it up because it is specific, dated, and argues against the vendor's own interest — but it is not a primary source.
- **Anything about your actual current profile.** LinkedIn blocks automated fetching, so every statement about your headline, follower count or your sister's posts came from the briefing rather than from my own observation. Re-check by eye before acting.

### Two open questions only you can close

1. **What is Pramaan?** It occupies the highest-value seven characters on your profile and nobody established what it is. Three dimensions of this research flagged it independently and all three refused to assume.
2. **What does your appointment letter say your designation is?** Every title recommendation in Section 2 forks on that string.
